title: Wireless millikelvin interconnects for superconducting quantum hardware
authors: Kristopher Barr, Mingyan Zhong, Euan Parry, Manoj Stanley, Qusay Al-Taai, Paniz Foshat, Kaveh Delfanazari, Martin Weides, Nick M. Ridler, Chong Li, Alessandro Rossi
abstract: Scalable quantum computing is limited by the dense network of electrical interconnects linking cryogenic quantum processors to room-temperature control electronics. To overcome this bottleneck, considerable effort has focused on cryogenic CMOS electronics and microwave-to-optical transduction, aiming to reduce wiring complexity and thermal loading. Wireless interconnects have recently emerged as a promising complementary approach, yet their compatibility with superconducting quantum hardware remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate the wireless excitation of a superconducting microwave resonator of the type routinely employed for qubit readout, operating at millikelvin temperatures inside a dilution refrigerator. By directly comparing wired and wireless operation within the same cryogenic environment, we show that wireless coupling preserves the intrinsic resonator response while revealing parasitic electromagnetic pathways arising from stray radiation within the cryostat enclosure. These results establish a framework for the co-design of wireless interconnects, cryogenic packaging and superconducting quantum hardware.
summary: This paper demonstrates that wireless microwave interconnects can successfully excite superconducting resonators at millikelvin temperatures, offering a path to overcome wiring density limitations in quantum computing. By comparing results to traditional wired links, the authors validate the feasibility of free-space coupling while also characterizing unavoidable parasitic losses from stray radiation within the cryostat. The findings establish critical design guidelines for integrating wireless components into future scalable quantum hardware.
main_problem: Scalability of quantum computing is bottlenecked by dense electrical interconnects, necessitating a reliable wireless link solution for cryogenic hardware.
main_result: Wireless excitation preserves the intrinsic superconducting resonator response compared to wired links, establishing a framework for co-designing such interconnects despite residual stray radiation losses.
method: The authors experimentally compare microwave resonator characterization using both direct wiring and free-space wireless coupling within a dilution refrigerator environment.
model_or_system: The system involves superconducting microwave resonators (DUT) patterned on NbN film, measured at millikelvin temperatures. The interconnect uses planar antennas and metalens optics to guide microwaves through cryostat apertures.
key_observables: Resonant frequency ($f_r$), internal quality factor ($Q_i$), transmission coefficient ($	ext{|S}_{21}|$), and temperature dependence of these parameters.
important_parameters: Operating temperatures ranging from $20 	ext{ mK}$ to $3.0 	ext{ K}$; input power in the few-photon regime (approx. $-116 	ext{ dBm}$).
main_assumptions: The study assumes that wireless coupling can be engineered to match the intrinsic response of superconducting hardware, though residual stray radiation remains a challenge.
figures_summary: Figures show schematic setups for wireless links, $	ext{|S}_{21}|$ spectra comparing wired vs. wireless modes across temperatures, and analyses detailing stray loss mechanisms and the effect of RF absorbers on signal quality.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the interconnect bottleneck to demonstrating successful wireless excitation, characterizing the resulting losses (stray radiation), and finally proposing a co-design framework incorporating packaging and material science solutions.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the physical engineering challenges of scaling quantum processors by providing empirical data on microwave coupling in extreme cryogenic environments, which is crucial for building large quantum systems.
